JsonString: {"unit_id": "unit01", "section": "section_a", "title": "Connection or conversation", "type": "reading", "passage": "A campus conversation club met each Thursday in a room that looked out over the library courtyard. Its members could send a message in seconds, yet during shared breaks some sat together without knowing how to begin. Several said they felt lonely even while their screens filled with names, photos, and alerts. The club asked a practical question: what kind of connection does this moment need? To explore it, student organizers designed a four-week listening experiment for learning, not a scientific study. At each session, members placed their devices in a basket for twenty minutes and took turns describing a small challenge. The listener had to ask one follow-up question and summarize what they had heard before replying. The rule felt awkward at first, and some participants were anxious that an urgent message might arrive. By the third session, a pause no longer seemed like a failure; it gave people time to choose words carefully. Members began noticing tone, hesitation, and the meaning behind a brief answer. They did not stop using group chats or video calls, which remained useful for planning and maintaining distant friendships. A quick digital message worked well when information was simple and time was short. A face-to-face conversation offered something different: people could revise an idea, respond to emotion, and build trust. The club's notes described its own practice, not proof that every student needed the same routine. That limit made the experiment more useful, because it invited discussion instead of imposing a universal rule. Readiness for the digital age therefore means choosing a tool with a purpose, rather than treating every notification as a command. On busy days, members used a shared calendar to protect an uninterrupted study session. On difficult days, they put phones away and asked a friend to listen before giving advice. Their goal was not less technology, but more intentional communication and a clearer sense of when to converse. Each Thursday ended with one question: did today's connection help someone feel understood?"}

Name: unit01:section_b
JsonString: {"unit_id": "unit01", "section": "section_b", "title": "Living in the digital world", "type": "reading", "passage": "For many students, the digital world begins before breakfast, when a notification lights up a device beside the bed. A student may intend to check one message and then scroll through a platform for several minutes. An algorithm filters the feed, quietly deciding which stories appear again and which disappear. Because the stream feels personal, users can mistake repeated exposure for a balanced view of the world. That is why digital literacy starts with attention: notice what a platform asks you to do, and decide whether it deserves the next minute. A first-year class tested a simple habit plan for two weeks, keeping short notes on when they checked screens during study. They found that opening a device between tasks often made it harder to return to the original question. Trying to multitask did not remove the work; it scattered the attention needed to understand complex ideas. The students began grouping messages into set check-in times and placing one offline study block on their daily schedule. One student found virtual study groups useful, provided that members agreed on a goal before joining. Another reviewed privacy settings after learning how much information a default profile could reveal. A cyber safety instructor asked the class to treat each link, password request, and public post as a choice with consequences. The lesson was not to fear every platform but to understand how its tools filter information and shape habits. When a data leak or unwanted contact occurs, prevention is valuable; afterwards, calm reporting and account changes matter too. Students also discussed screen addiction without using the term as a casual label for every long evening online. A habit becomes concerning when it repeatedly harms sleep, learning, or relationships and a person cannot easily adjust it. Restored balance came from small changes: a mindful walk between lectures, a device-free meal, and a clear end time for study. During an offline hour, roommates noticed more interaction and solved small disagreements before they grew. These routines did not make the internet less powerful; they helped students use it more deliberately. Living well online is not a contest to stay disconnected, but a practice of protecting attention, privacy, and human presence."}

Name: unit01:section_c
JsonString: {"unit_id": "unit01", "section": "section_c", "title": "Stories of China", "type": "stories_of_china", "passage": "This original practice story is set in a fictional mountain county, where the nearest specialist clinic is several hours from some villages. A local health center wanted older residents to receive advice without turning every checkup into a long journey. It partnered with doctors in a coastal teaching hospital and used a secure telemedicine platform to review basic scans. The small team added a familiar phone and a private room so patients could ask questions with a nurse nearby. At first, the technology was only one part of a bigger plan. Local staff helped residents learn how to place the device, describe symptoms, and ask for a second explanation. When a connection failed, the center recorded questions and arranged a call-back instead of pretending the screen had solved everything. Doctors reviewed images carefully and sent written guidance to local clinicians, who remained responsible for follow-up care. A daughter living far away could join one appointment, but the patient still chose what information to share. The process respected privacy as well as distance. This fictional example does not claim that every village has the same service or that online advice can replace an examination. It shows why human communication matters when a new tool enters healthcare. The clinic kept an offline option for people who lacked a suitable phone, steady signal, or confidence using an app. Volunteers explained how the service worked, while medical staff checked whether the advice was clear and useful. Gradually, families spent less time arranging travel for routine questions and more time planning care with local professionals. The change depended on trust, accessible design, and patient choice rather than on a device alone. Stories of China can include this kind of practical innovation: people using knowledge and technology to solve a local need. Its value is measured not by how advanced a screen looks, but by whether residents can participate safely. A shared project becomes stronger when city doctors, county clinicians, families, and public services each take a clear role. In that sense, digital progress is a human achievement: it expands connection while keeping dignity, responsibility, and community in view."}

Name: unit02:section_a
JsonString: {"unit_id": "unit02", "section": "section_a", "title": "Two Lives, One Lesson", "type": "reading", "passage": "The class opened an exhibit called Lives in Motion in the campus archive, where biographies were read as sequences of choices. Its task was not to rank remarkable people, but to ask which evidence could explain a turning point. One case followed Zheng He, the explorer whose fleet traveled across Indian Ocean routes in the early fifteenth century. Another introduced Audrey Hepburn, whose public portrait later became linked to a humanitarian mission for children. Though the lives belonged to different eras and different professions, students searched for a shared question: what does service require? The first group placed maps and port names beside a short narrative of the voyage. Records show that trade goods moved across sea routes, yet a map cannot tell every story of the people along them. Students marked documented details in blue and their own interpretations in amber. This color code helped them witness the difference between a source and a conclusion. It also kept the display from presenting one simple motive as the whole explanation. In the second case, the class examined why an ambitious performer might use fame to draw attention to children's needs. They learned that Hepburn served UNICEF as Goodwill Ambassador and traveled to Ethiopia in 1988 to highlight the drought's effects. Her work did not mean one visitor could solve a complex crisis. It showed how compassion and sustained attention could support a wider humanitarian effort. Students compared what the sources stated with what a reader might only infer. When they turned to the final wall, neither figure seemed like a ready-made model for every life. The students could admire particular choices without treating a famous person as perfect. They described a legacy as influence people inherit, question, and sometimes continue in new ways. The exhibit's narrative joined evidence, context, and consequences instead of relying on a dramatic portrait. Each visitor left with one question about ambition, responsibility, and the next action they could take."}

Name: unit02:section_b
JsonString: {"unit_id": "unit02", "section": "section_b", "title": "Audrey Hepburn — a real angel in the world", "type": "reading", "passage": "Students built an original exhibit about Audrey Hepburn, and they started with the familiar elegant portrait on a screen. The image opened a door, but it could not tell visitors everything about a life. A biography becomes richer when it places public work beside career and context. Their teacher asked them to separate documented events from assumptions about a famous person's private thoughts. That rule turned the display into a lesson in evidence, not a shrine. The class added one verified fact: Hepburn served as a UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador. In 1988 she traveled to Ethiopia to raise awareness of drought affecting children and women. Her mission brought a humanitarian concern into view, but did not claim that one person could end a crisis. Students explained why a public witness can help an audience notice a problem. They also asked whose experience should be heard first: the people living with that problem. A local organization may understand needs that an outsider cannot see from a brief visit. For that reason, charity work needs listening, accountability, and long-term partnership as well as attention. Compassion is not a decoration added to a portrait; it is a reason to respond thoughtfully. Supporting a humanitarian mission also requires perseverance, because public attention alone cannot sustain long-term work. They admired her devotion without claiming that fame guarantees wisdom. The discussion made one tension visible: publicity can open a door, yet it can also simplify people's lives. Students revised their headline to include both career and service. A second panel told how readers can check dates and original sources before repeating a claim. Instead of copying a dramatic quotation, they wrote a precise summary and named the source. The exhibit closed by asking visitors to find one responsible action that could inspire others in their community."}

Name: unit02:section_c

Their guide explained that historians describe seven expeditions across the Indian Ocean in the early fifteenth century. The students began with a fleet route and traced the names of ports recorded in maps and written accounts. The archive showed that the voyages carried goods including silk, porcelain, medicines, and metal objects to trading ports. A route map helped them imagine distance, but also reminded them that maps select what to show. The group labeled locations and directions before drawing any conclusion about the purpose of a stop. Each stop was discussed as a place where people met, exchanged goods, and made decisions. Trade is one documented purpose, and historical records can reveal how maritime networks connected regions. However, no single map can witness every conversation or explain every participant's experience. The learners compared a chart with written descriptions rather than treating either source as complete. This practice made the lesson more remarkable than memorizing a list of destinations. One student asked whether a modern reader should admire a voyage without asking difficult questions. The class agreed that respect for achievement and careful criticism can exist together. They separated evidence about routes from broader claims about what every encounter meant. That distinction kept the story open to more than one question. A voyage can reveal planning, navigation, and exchange, while still leaving gaps in the record. The fleet's legacy is therefore a useful subject for comparing past and present ideas of connection. The class placed a route-map model beside a note about how historical knowledge is built. The display invited visitors to follow an explorer's path, then inspect the sources that support the narrative. At the exit, each learner wrote one question inspired by the map and one fact they could verify."}

Name: unit03:section_a
JsonString: {"unit_id": "unit03", "section": "section_a", "title": "The Surprising Purpose of Travel", "type": "reading", "passage": "Many students imagine a successful trip as reaching a famous destination, taking clear photos, and returning without delay. Their itinerary lists landmarks in order, while a light bag of luggage keeps every step efficient. A campus travel seminar asked whether this plan explains what a journey can change. Its learners compared three journals rather than treating one traveler as a model for everyone. They found that travel also depends on curiosity: noticing details that a hurried schedule might hide. One journal belonged to a solo traveler whose train connection was cancelled before departure. Instead of calling the day a failure, she used a map to navigate a nearby neighborhood. She chose a quieter route, asked a local bookshop owner for directions, and began to wander. That brief encounter led to a conversation about the river, old streets, and everyday work. The new landscape became memorable not because it was famous, but because she had paid attention. Another student preferred a hostel where guests shared a kitchen and could exchange practical advice. She had made a reservation for the first night, yet left the following morning open. When rain blocked the footpath, the group had to adapt rather than force the original plan. A covered market gave them shelter, a warm drink, and time to compare their expectations. Their conversation shifted perspective: unfamiliar places were not puzzles to conquer but communities to meet. The seminar did not suggest that planning or safety checks were unnecessary. It recommended a flexible itinerary, reliable contacts, and enough time to reflect after an unexpected change. Students wrote one question about what they hoped to learn before choosing a destination. Later, they described how each detour could transform their attention to ordinary life at home. Their conclusion was simple: a meaningful journey is measured by what you notice and reconsider."}

Name: unit03:section_b
JsonString: {"unit_id": "unit03", "section": "section_b", "title": "Traveling Solo: Room to Adapt", "type": "reading", "passage": "Mei had traveled with family before, but her first solo departure made a familiar station feel enormous. She checked her reservation twice, placed a small card with the hostel address in her pocket, and told her sister when she expected to arrive. Packing light luggage let her keep one hand free for her ticket and phone. She had expected confidence to arrive before the trip began, but it came in smaller decisions. At the platform, she felt nervous and reminded herself why she had chosen to go. Her itinerary named the hostel and one museum, while leaving the afternoon unplanned. After checking in, she asked the desk clerk which streets remained busy before dusk. The clerk marked a simple route to a market and advised her to avoid a closed riverside path. Mei used the map to navigate the first turns, then put it away to notice shop signs and sounds. When she missed a turning, she did not pretend to understand the route. A local bookseller showed her a safer street and asked what she hoped to see. That encounter became a memorable conversation about the neighborhood's changing shops. Mei began to wander slowly, choosing a public square rather than chasing a distant destination. A sudden rain shower made the shortest path slippery, so she adapted and waited under a covered stall. The landscape looked different from beneath the awning, and a shop owner offered tea while the rain passed. By returning to the hostel before dusk, Mei kept her trip both open and sensible. Her journal noted that independence does not require refusing help. She had once thought a fixed itinerary was the only protection from uncertainty. Now she would rather ask a respectful question than follow a confusing route alone. The journey transformed her perspective: solo travel could combine preparation, curiosity, and trust."}

Name: unit03:section_c
JsonString: {"unit_id": "unit03", "section": "section_c", "title": "Stories of China", "type": "stories_of_china", "passage": "In an original practice story, Lin leaves Chengdu for Xi'an on a high-speed train to meet her cousin. She has visited stations with classmates, but never studied a route as part of a reading assignment. Before departure, her teacher asks each traveler to note one expectation and one question. Lin expects a quick arrival and plans to photograph the station architecture. She carries light luggage, a notebook, and an itinerary with an afternoon left open. Across the aisle, a retired teacher is traveling to visit an old friend. They compare the route with the places each hopes to see, without claiming one person's plan is better. Their encounter begins with a question about the landscape beyond the window. The teacher describes how moving between cities has changed the work and family routines of people she knows. Lin listens, then adds the story to her notes rather than treating it as a universal rule. As the train continues, fields, rivers, and denser neighborhoods appear in sequence. The shifting landscape helps her notice that a route connects places without making them identical. She uses a map to follow the journey and ask how people navigate changes in daily life. A station announcement changes the arrival track, and passengers adapt calmly to new directions. Lin checks her destination, follows signs, and helps another traveler locate the correct platform. Later, her cousin shows her a street market that does not appear on the short itinerary. The local vendors explain how seasonal choices shape what they sell, and Lin asks permission before taking a photo. The trip's memorable moments come from conversations as much as scenery. On returning, Lin says travel can transform perspective when curiosity is joined to respect. Her class concludes that transport infrastructure offers a path, but people give the journey meaning."}

Name: unit04:section_a
JsonString: {"unit_id": "unit04", "section": "section_a", "title": "What Makes Work Meaningful?", "type": "reading", "passage": "At a campus career workshop, students gathered around a question that sounded simple but unsettled them: what makes work meaningful? The facilitator wrote worker and laborer on the board, then asked whether either word could measure a person's worth. One student associated laborer with strength and routine, while another imagined worker as someone who made decisions. The instructor warned that this attitude can quietly rank people before anyone understands what their jobs require. A task may be physical, repetitive, or performed behind the scenes, yet still demand close attention. The group visited a campus service team and watched a worker prepare a busy study room. She followed a routine checklist, but she also noticed a loose chair and stopped to report it. A student asked whether that extra judgment was part of the occupation or simply personal kindness. The worker explained that safety and dignity often depend on small decisions no checklist can predict. Later, a violin maker invited the class into a workshop. He asked his apprentice to compare two joints that looked almost identical. With careful precision, the apprentice measured the narrow gap that could alter the instrument's sound. The demonstration did not make one occupation more valuable than another; instead, it showed how knowledge and responsibility shape the quality of work. Back at the workshop, the students revised their first definitions and saw that skill can grow inside a routine and that craft is not limited to objects displayed in galleries. The instructor asked everyone to name one contribution they had previously overlooked. Students mentioned cleaners, repairers, cooks, and laboratory assistants. Each example required different knowledge, but each could protect another person's time, safety, or trust. The discussion ended without ranking the jobs, and the students agreed that meaningful work is not defined by a title alone. Pride becomes durable when people take responsibility for quality and treat those affected by their work with respect. That kind of fulfillment can belong to many occupations."}

Name: unit04:section_b
JsonString: {"unit_id": "unit04", "section": "section_b", "title": "A Craft Tradition, Practiced with Care", "type": "reading", "passage": "When Lin first entered the violin workshop, the master gave the apprentice a repair that seemed almost finished. A narrow joint still needed attention, although it was difficult to see without a lamp, so the master asked Lin to measure it twice and explain what the numbers meant. Lin wanted to hurry because a customer was waiting, but the master reminded him that a beautiful surface could hide a weak connection. A gap that was too wide might change the instrument's sound and shorten the repair's life. Lin repeated the measurement, adjusted the piece, and tested the fit before using glue. The routine felt slow, yet each step answered a different question about strength and balance. The master explained that precision was not perfection for its own sake; it was a promise about how the instrument would perform. Months later, Lin began to teach the same routine to a new apprentice. He kept the useful checks but also tried a digital gauge beside the workshop's older tool. Rather than accepting novelty or rejecting it, he compared the readings and asked whether the new method made the result clearer. When it did, he recorded the procedure so the whole team could use it. His dedication grew through repeated practice, and his passion became visible in how carefully he explained mistakes. A customer returned after hearing the repaired violin in a small concert. She thanked Lin not only for restoring the sound but also for describing what had been changed. That honest conversation strengthened trust between the workshop and its neighbors. Lin understood that tradition was not a command to repeat every motion forever. It was a body of knowledge carried forward, examined, and improved when evidence justified a change. The craft would remain rewarding only if young workers could learn, question, and contribute. In the final lesson of the day, the master asked Lin to name the standard he hoped to pass on. Lin answered: protect the work, respect the person who depends on it, and pursue excellence without confusing speed with skill."}

Name: unit04:section_c
JsonString: {"unit_id": "unit04", "section": "section_c", "title": "Stories of China", "type": "stories_of_china", "passage": "In this original learning story, a student named Mei visits a small silk-embroidery workshop in Suzhou with her class. She expects to see finished patterns, but the guide introduces the artisans who prepare the threads and study the designs, and Mei notices that a flower is not copied by counting colors alone. Each maker considers how a line turns, where the fabric will be used, and which details must remain clear. An artisan invites the students to look closely at a sample under a lamp. Mei records the explanation and asks before taking a photograph. The group learns that respect begins by listening to the people who hold the knowledge. At the next table, an apprentice practices a short row of stitches. Her mentor corrects the angle gently and asks her to describe what changed. The repeated exercise is not empty routine; it trains the hand to control tension and the eye to notice uneven thread. The student sees that heritage is carried by people who work, teach, and make decisions today. Later, the team discusses a new design for a community exhibition. They keep a familiar motif but adjust its size so visitors can see the stitch pattern from a distance. The change is reviewed with the makers rather than imposed by the visitors. Mei asks how the workshop can make this labor sustainable. The guide explains that fair payment, credit for makers, and opportunities to teach matter as much as displaying beautiful objects. Before leaving, each student chooses one question to investigate instead of claiming to understand the whole craft in an afternoon. Mei writes that an occupation can create income and also protect a shared memory. Her class understands that dignity is not supplied by praise alone; it grows when skilled people can make choices and be recognized for them. The visit changes their idea of tradition: it is not a silent object behind glass, but living knowledge practiced with care, renewed with permission, and shared across generations. These stories of China show how meaningful work can connect personal skill, community identity, and a future that still has room to change."}

When one reading falls outside its expected range, engineers compare it with other data before changing course. The purpose of a test is not to prove a design perfect but to learn whether it works under specified conditions. Lin wrote down the claim, the evidence, and the uncertainty instead of trusting the brightest image. At the display, an animation showed the relay passing a message between the far-side probe and Earth. Lin followed the signal route with his finger and saw how cooperation joined operators, scientists, and equipment across distance. Students next received sample data and had to decide which model site was level enough for a safe descent. Two groups disagreed because they had used different reference points on the same slope. When they compared their methods, they found that one sensor had been read from the wrong scale. Lin revised his answer and explained why the corrected evidence changed the landing choice. He left with a more ambitious idea of exploration: each generation inherits not only a dream, but a method for checking it."}

Name: unit06:section_a
JsonString: {"unit_id": "unit06", "section": "section_a", "title": "Surviving an economic crisis", "type": "reading", "passage": "In the old harbor district, Lantern Books had served students for twenty years, but a recession changed the street. Inflation pushed up rent and delivery costs, while a tight budget left fewer new titles on its shelves. Owner Mei wrote each expense beside the supply of books and the demand from readers instead of guessing. Her savings covered only two months, and she feared the shop would close before the next school term. To understand the crisis, she asked customers what they needed and what they could afford. A campus club suggested a sharing wall where a reader could leave one book and choose another. Mei took a small loan to build weatherproof shelves and a simple checkout desk. During a two-week pilot, every exchange was entered in a paper ledger with a fair, affordable fee. The club recorded the book condition, the reader's choice, and the time each title remained on the shelf. The early numbers showed that a few popular subjects moved quickly while other titles waited. Rather than call the project an instant success, Mei compared its modest revenue with saved purchasing costs. Reusing books improved efficiency, but cleaning, sorting, and missing-copy checks still required staff time. Some consumers could not pay even a small fee, so the club created a no-fee exchange hour. The change widened access without hiding the real cost of keeping the service open. Mei explained that sharing works only when rules protect both the resource and the people using it. By the end of the term, the shop had not become rich, yet it had kept two local jobs and reopened a quiet reading corner. Readers returned with suggestions, and the club helped repair damaged covers instead of discarding every copy. This modest resilience came from trust, clear records, and repeated adjustments rather than one heroic investment. Students traced how price, supply, demand, and access shaped ordinary choices in the neighborhood. They left with a practical lesson: a healthy economy depends on choices that keep value circulating and responsibility visible."}

Name: unit06:section_b
JsonString: {"unit_id": "unit06", "section": "section_b", "title": "The sharing economy turns a new page with books", "type": "reading", "passage": "On campus, a club found that students often bought a required book for one term and then let it collect dust. They designed a sharing exchange where members could lend or swap a copy through a staffed locker. The organizers called it Page Loop, an original student startup built to expand access, not promise instant revenue. Before opening, they surveyed consumers about prices, titles, and whether a refundable deposit felt fair. The team revised the model: a small affordable charge covered checks, while members could volunteer during free-access hours. A barcode, condition note, and clear return date let volunteers track supply without treating every user as a risk. During a month-long trial, they logged which titles moved, which stayed untouched, and when the line grew. Demand shifted around exam weeks, so the club added high-use titles and asked departments to donate older editions. The records also revealed a bottleneck: volunteers spent too long checking books at a single desk. They arranged two return boxes and a short inspection rota, improving efficiency without removing a human check. One sponsor suggested rapid expansion, but the club compared extra staffing and repair costs first. The new site would add reach, yet could weaken local support if no partner helped maintain the books. A teacher asked the group to distinguish activity from impact: more loans did not automatically mean fairer access. Members compared user feedback, wait times, damaged copies, and costs before changing the rules. They kept a free weekly hour for students who could not pay, supported by a campus fund. During that hour, exchange still followed the same condition and return standards. After one term, the project had modest revenue and stronger ties between the club and the campus shop. The team described the model as sustainable only if access, maintenance, and local cooperation remained in balance. Page Loop taught them that sharing works best when transparency makes responsibility as visible as convenience."}

Name: unit06:section_c
JsonString: {"unit_id": "unit06", "section": "section_c", "title": "Stories of China: A Fictional County Library Case", "type": "stories_of_china", "passage": "For a class project, students created a fictional county case called Yunhe to examine access to reading during a downturn. In their story, many families had a tight budget, and the county library could not buy every new title. The students proposed a shared digital-lending catalog so one licensed copy could reach more readers over time.
